blocks.text: Split an interactive feature into a model for state and rules, a view for display, and a controller for input.

The **model** owns data and business rules and knows nothing about the screen. The **view** renders model state. The **controller** translates user input into model operations. A change in the model reaches the view through notification, not through the controller.
Server-side web frameworks use a variant: the controller selects a model and a view per request, with no live notifications.

walkthrough.note: The model owns the target temperature and the clamping rule. It announces changes through a listener interface and has no import of any view.
The view implements the listener and renders. It holds no rules and sends no commands to the model.
The controller maps raw input to model operations. It does not format output or repeat the clamping rule.
Wiring registers the view as a model listener and gives the controller the model. The view and controller never reference each other.

blocks.text: Server-rendered account pages in a web portal.

In a request-driven MVC framework the controller receives `GET /accounts/42`, asks the domain model for the account, adds it to the `Model` map and names a template. The template only renders. Changing the page layout never touches the account rules, and a JSON endpoint reuses the same model with a different view.

lists.title: Use when
items: The same state needs several presentations or input paths.
UI-free rules should be tested without a screen.
A framework already structures requests as controller plus view.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: A reactive UI with rich bindings fits [MVVM](kata:mvvm) better.
The screen is trivial and has no rules worth isolating.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: The controller grows into a God class that holds business rules.
The view reads from many models and recomputes rules.
The model calling a view method directly, which breaks the dependency direction.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: One controller, view and model per button.
Controllers that only forward to a service and return a view name.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records make immutable view models that templates read but cannot mutate.
Pattern-matching `switch` over sealed command types gives controllers exhaustive input handling.

rows.difference: MVVM replaces the controller with a view model that exposes state and commands, and the view binds to it declaratively. MVC's view is usually updated through code.
MVC uses Observer so the model can notify views without referencing them. Observer is one mechanism; MVC is the three-role split.
A controller coordinates model and view like a mediator, but its main job is translating input; a mediator manages peer-to-peer collaboration.
MVC usually lives inside the presentation layer, with the model drawing on the business layer below.

exercises.scenario: A server-rendered admin portal: each request needs to read some domain state, choose a template and return HTML. There is no client-side data binding and pages are stateless between requests.

options.why: Controllers handle the request, the model supplies data and a template renders it: the request-driven variant fits.
MVVM depends on long-lived bindings between view and view model, which a stateless request cycle lacks.
Nothing needs to be pushed to subscribers; each page is built once per request.
There are no peer components to decouple; the problem is separating roles in the request flow.

modelAnswer.text: The model holds state and rules and has no UI knowledge. The view renders model state. The controller turns user input into model calls. The model notifies registered views when it changes, so the view never depends on the controller and the model never depends on the view.

keyPoints: Changes reach the view via notification
